applicableAreas: western site boundary where overhead electric line is present
areas within 15 feet of overhead distribution conductor
findings.observation: Sheet 21 documents an existing overhead electric line (OHE) running along the western boundary with utility poles and a service transition to underground infrastructure. Sheet 31 (landscape plan) shows the OHE line and depicts trees positioned along the site boundary near this overhead line. Sheet 35 provides a plant schedule listing proposed tree species: 10 Cedar Elm (Ulmus Crassifolia), 2 Live Oak (Quercus Virginiana), 6 Mexican Redbud (Cercis Canadensis var. Mexicana), and 2 Texas Mountain Laurel (Sophora Secundiflora). However, the plant schedule does not indicate the utility-compatible (UC) status of any species per ECM Appendix F, and no clearance dimensions are provided on the landscape plan to verify distances from these species to the outside conductor.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.10.10.4 requires that only utility-compatible trees (marked UC in ECM Appendix F) be proposed within 15 feet of distribution conductors. The landscape plan shows trees near the overhead line, but: (1) the voltage classification of the OHE line (distribution vs. transmission) is not documented on the plans; (2) the plant schedule provides species names but does not reference ECM Appendix F or identify UC status for any proposed species; (3) no clearance dimensions are shown to verify compliance with the 15-foot minimum for distribution. Without documented UC status from ECM Appendix F and without clearance dimensions, it cannot be determined whether proposed non-utility-compatible species are located within 15 feet of the outside conductor.
findings.comment: Plant schedule lists tree species proposed near overhead electric line, but does not document utility-compatible (UC) status per ECM Appendix F required by UCM § 1.10.10.4. Clearance distances from tree trunks to outside conductors are not dimensioned on landscape plan, preventing verification of compliance with 15-foot minimum distance for non-utility-compatible species near distribution conductors.

applicableAreas: western and southern site boundaries where overhead electric lines are present
areas within 25 feet of overhead distribution conductor
findings.observation: Sheet 31 (landscape plan) shows overhead electric lines (OHE) running along site boundaries with utility poles, and trees positioned along these boundaries. Sheet 32 (tree inventory) documents surveyed trees on site including large native species: Live Oak specimens with DBH of 32 inches (Tree 4018), 36 inches (Tree 4026), 27 inches (Tree 4027), and 24 inches (Tree 4038), all marked as Appendix F species; Cedar Elm 17 inches DBH (Tree 4010); Pecan 24 inches DBH (Tree 4015). These large DBH trees typically have mature heights exceeding 40 feet (Live Oak and Cedar Elm commonly 40-60 feet). Sheet 35 specifies proposed planting of 10 Cedar Elm and 2 Live Oak. The landscape plan shows multiple tree symbols positioned directly adjacent to or overlapping the OHE line along the southern boundary (per vision analysis: '3+ trees positioned directly underneath or extremely close to the OHE line'). However, the landscape plan provides NO clearance dimensions from tree trunks to the outside conductor, and the plant schedule does NOT specify mature heights or indicate which species are 'large trees' (40+ feet per ECM Appendix F).
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.10.10.4 requires that large trees (mature height 40 feet or greater per ECM Appendix F) be positioned at least 25 feet from the outside conductor of overhead distribution facilities. The site has: (1) documented large native trees (Live Oak, Cedar Elm) with diameters typically correlating to 40+ foot mature heights; (2) proposed plantings of the same large species (Live Oak, Cedar Elm); (3) trees visually positioned adjacent to or overlapping the overhead line on site boundary; and (4) NO clearance dimensions dimensioning the distance from tree trunk center to outside conductor to verify the 25-foot minimum. The failure to document mature heights on the plant schedule prevents verification of which species qualify as 'large trees,' and the absence of clearance dimensions on the landscape plan means the 25-foot setback cannot be verified.
findings.comment: Large trees (Live Oak and Cedar Elm) with typical mature heights of 40-50 feet are shown on landscape plan and tree survey adjacent to overhead distribution conductors. Plans do not document mature heights to identify large trees (40+ feet per ECM Appendix F), and no clearance dimensions are provided to verify compliance with 25-foot minimum setback from distribution conductor.

applicableAreas: western site boundary where utility poles are located along overhead electric line
findings.observation: Sheet 21 (electrical plan) shows existing overhead electric line (OHE) running north-south along the western boundary with utility poles represented by small circular symbols. Sheet 31 (landscape plan) depicts the OHE line with poles along the southern boundary and trees positioned along the boundaries where poles are located. Vision analysis of Sheet 31 states: 'several proposed trees positioned along the southern boundary that appear to be placed directly underneath or extremely close to the overhead electric line' and notes 'poles are positioned along this OHE line.' However, no clearance dimensions are provided on the landscape plan documenting the distance from tree trunk center to the nearest utility pole.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.10.10.4 establishes a 10-foot lateral distance minimum from tree trunk center to any overhead electric utility pole. Utility poles are documented on both the electrical plan and landscape plan along the overhead line. Trees are shown on the landscape plan positioned near these boundaries where poles are present. However, without clearance dimensions on the landscape plan, it cannot be confirmed whether the proposed and retained trees maintain the required 10-foot minimum distance from the pole. The vision tool noted trees appearing 'directly underneath or extremely close to' the OHE line, suggesting possible violations, but precise distances cannot be verified from available evidence.
findings.comment: Utility poles present along overhead electric line at property boundaries. Landscape plan shows trees positioned near poles but provides no clearance dimensions to verify 10-foot minimum distance from tree trunk to pole.

applicableAreas: landscape plan and plant schedule area
findings.observation: Sheet 31 (landscape plan) includes a plant legend identifying tree types by abbreviation (SY=Street Yard, PL=Parking Lot, P=Parking Buffer, M=Mitigation) but does not indicate species identification or mature height specifications. Sheet 35 (plant schedule) provides a plant list with species names and botanical names: Live Oak (Quercus Virginiana), Cedar Elm (Ulmus Crassifolia), Texas Mountain Laurel (Sophora Secundiflora), Mexican Redbud (Cercis Canadensis var. Mexicana), and various shrubs and groundcovers. However, the plant legend on the landscape plan does not cross-reference these species to allow field verification during plant inspection. The plant schedule specifies container size and caliper at planting but not mature height, and does not indicate utility-compatible (UC) designation from ECM Appendix F.
findings.reasoning: Per Reviewer Convention, when trees are proposed near electric facilities, the landscape plan and plant legend must identify the species of all trees near utilities to allow field verification during construction that the correct species have been planted and to verify compliance with utility-compatibility requirements per UCM § 1.10.10.4. Sheet 31 shows trees with symbols (SY, PL, P, M designations) but the plant legend does not identify which species corresponds to each symbol location. This prevents a field inspector from confirming that the correct species have been planted at each location. Additionally, neither the landscape plan nor plant schedule documents the utility-compatible (UC) status required by ECM Appendix F for species proposed within utility clearance zones.
findings.comment: Plant legend on landscape plan does not identify species of trees proposed near overhead electric facilities, and plant schedule does not reference ECM Appendix F utility-compatible (UC) designations. Field verification of proper species installation cannot be performed.

applicableAreas: landscape plan and plant schedule for areas within clearance zones of overhead electric facilities
findings.observation: Sheet 35 lists proposed shade trees (Live Oak 100 gal., Cedar Elm 100 gal.) and ornamental trees (Texas Mountain Laurel 45 gal., Mexican Redbud 45 gal.) with minimum specifications at planting (4 inch caliper for shade trees; 2.5 inch caliper for ornamental trees). Sheet 35 also provides a tree inventory showing existing large trees: Live Oak specimens ranging from 12 to 42 inches DBH, Cedar Elm 17 inches DBH. However, the plant schedule specifies planting-size caliper only (4-inch, 2.5-inch) and does not indicate MATURE HEIGHT for any species. Without documented mature heights in the plant schedule, it cannot be determined which trees qualify as 'large trees' (40+ feet per ECM Appendix F) requiring stricter clearance distances (25 feet from distribution, 50 feet from transmission). The landscape plan does not differentiate or call out large tree locations.
findings.reasoning: Per Reviewer Convention and UCM § 1.10.10.4, large trees (mature height 40 feet or greater) have different clearance requirements from smaller trees: 25 feet from distribution conductors vs. 15 feet for other trees; 50 feet from transmission vs. 50 feet for all trees. For inspectors and subsequent reviewers to verify that the proposed plantings and retained trees comply with these differential requirements, the landscape plan must explicitly identify which trees are 'large' (40+ feet mature height). The plant schedule must document mature heights per ECM Appendix F for each species proposed in clearance zones. Currently, the plans provide only planting-size specifications (caliper/container size) without mature height annotation, preventing differentiation of large vs. non-large trees.
findings.comment: Landscape plan and plant schedule do not document mature heights (per ECM Appendix F) for proposed and retained tree species, preventing identification of 'large trees' (40+ feet) requiring stricter 25-foot setbacks from distribution conductors.

applicableAreas: landscape plan in relation to overhead electric facilities along site boundaries
findings.observation: Sheet 21 (electrical plan) documents an existing overhead electric line (OHE) along the western boundary with poles and transition to underground service. Sheet 31 (landscape plan) depicts the same property with an OHE line notation along the southern boundary and utility poles shown. Trees are shown on the landscape plan with various symbols (SY, PL, P, M) positioned near the boundaries where OHE lines are present. However, the landscape plan provides no dimensional grid, no cross-reference with the electrical plan, and no clearance annotations (distances, dimensions, or notes) relating the tree positions to the overhead conductors or poles. Vision analysis confirms: 'There are no clearance dimensions or notes regarding tree placement near overhead electric lines or other utilities provided on this specific sheet.'
findings.reasoning: Per Reviewer Convention, when overhead electric facilities are present or proposed, the landscape plan must display sufficient detail to allow verification of tree clearances from conductors. At a minimum, this requires: (1) overhead conductor locations and pole positions clearly shown in relation to tree locations; (2) clearance dimensions documenting distance from tree trunk center to outside conductor; (3) coordinate reference or clear spatial relationship allowing cross-reference with the utility/electrical plan. Currently, the landscape plan shows the OHE line notation and trees, but provides no dimensions, no notes confirming clearance distances, and no clear method for relating tree positions to conductor positions. An inspector cannot verify compliance with clearance zones without these dimensions.
findings.comment: Landscape plan shows overhead electric line and trees positioned near utility infrastructure, but provides no clearance dimensions, distance annotations, or cross-reference methodology to verify tree positions meet required setbacks from overhead conductors.

findings.observation: The Master Comment Report (Electric Review section, line 19) lists 'UCM § 1.10.10.3 & 4 - Customer Activity in Utility Easements - Landscaping & Trees' and references 'Appendix F of the Environmental Criteria Manual' as preliminary design requirements from Austin Energy. However, no Austin Energy approval letters, written exceptions, or variance documentation are present in the supplementary documents provided. The landscape plan shows proposed trees (Cedar Elm, Live Oak, Mexican Redbud, Texas Mountain Laurel) and depicts retained trees (including large Live Oak and Cedar Elm) positioned near or adjacent to the overhead electric line. The electrical plan indicates an existing overhead facility along the property boundary. No evidence of written approval from Austin Energy authorizing the placement of any tree within prohibited clearance zones is available in the submitted plans or comments.
findings.reasoning: UCM § 1.10.10.4 prohibits most non-utility-compatible trees and all large trees within defined clearance zones (15 feet for distribution non-UC trees, 25 feet for distribution large trees, 50 feet for transmission). The exception is for variations approved by 'explicit written approval from Austin Energy.' The landscape plan shows trees positioned adjacent to or very close to the documented overhead electric line, and the plant schedule lists species that may or may not be utility-compatible per ECM Appendix F. Without access to the full tree inventory with precise locations relative to conductors, and without documented mature heights, it cannot be definitively determined whether proposed or retained trees ARE in prohibited zones. However, the absence of any Austin Energy approval letters in the submitted documentation suggests that if trees are indeed in prohibited zones, required approval has not been obtained.
findings.comment: Landscape plan shows trees positioned near overhead electric infrastructure. No Austin Energy written approval letters are provided authorizing placement of trees within prohibited clearance zones. Verification of whether proposed or retained trees are within restricted zones cannot be completed from available evidence.
